column16: common_uses

Practicing a consciously selected way of responding in daily life. (draft); Reflecting on how a desired behavior could become more familiar and less effortful. (draft); Before a recurring situation, choose the response you want to practice making more automatic, such as pausing before answering. (reviewed); In a familiar social situation that repeatedly brings up an unwanted response, rehearse a preferred way of responding and later observe what happens. (reviewed); Practice a consistent starting routine for a daily activity so that the first step needs less deliberation. (reviewed); After identifying an unwanted habit, choose a specific replacement behavior to practice rather than focusing only on what to stop. (reviewed); Before a familiar sport or skill drill, rehearse the response you want to become more consistent under ordinary practice conditions. (reviewed)

Directed visualization of balanced brain and neck circulation. (draft); Reinforcing an intention toward clear, steady thinking without treating a medical condition. (draft); During a quiet wellness practice, direct attention toward a comfortable sense of steadiness in the head and neck without targeting a medical symptom. (reviewed); After mentally demanding work, use Brain Flow as a short reflective body-awareness exercise before returning to the task. (reviewed); Compare the experience of Brain Flow with Circulation as distinct practices; historical users described using these themes together. (reviewed); At rest after a physically demanding day, explore a sense of head-and-neck comfort as part of ordinary recovery. (reviewed); After Relax, bring attention to the Brain Flow intention during a calm, nonmedical self-care session. (reviewed)

Imagining smooth, comfortable circulation throughout the body. (draft); Exploring a felt sense of nourishment and vitality as a wellness practice, not a circulation treatment. (draft); While resting comfortably, explore the feeling or imagery of smooth circulation through your arms and legs. (reviewed); Following a long period of sitting, use Circulation as an optional awareness practice alongside ordinary movement breaks. (reviewed); Compare Circulation with Brain Flow to learn which purpose and imagery each function actually teaches. (reviewed); Include Circulation as a distinct optional practice when exploring the historical Tune-Up-centered self-care suggestions. (reviewed)

Practicing attention to a sense of physical ease. (draft); Exploring a calmer response to discomfort without ignoring symptoms or delaying appropriate care. (draft); In a safe, nonurgent situation involving familiar mild discomfort, practice shifting attention toward a sense of ease while remaining aware of symptoms. (reviewed); After Relax, use Comfort to explore a calmer relationship with everyday muscular tension. (reviewed); For an ordinary minor itch, explore the temporary comfort intention without ignoring a continuing or worsening cause. (reviewed); When minor familiar discomfort interferes with winding down, use Comfort as an optional settling practice before bedtime. (reviewed)

Visualizing the body's ordinary cleansing and maintenance processes. (draft); Reflecting on a sense of freshness and balance without claiming removal of toxins or replacing medical care. (draft); After an occasion of overeating or overindulgence, choose a gentle reset-oriented self-care intention without interpreting the practice as toxin removal. (reviewed)

Reflecting on the difference between a passing craving and a genuine need for nourishment. (draft); Practicing deliberate food choices while remaining responsive to hunger and nutritional needs. (draft); Before deciding to eat, pause and distinguish physical hunger from an automatic urge to snack. (reviewed); At a regular meal, practice noticing satisfaction and choosing an amount that meets your needs. (reviewed); Explore Appetite Choice alongside Nutricia in the historically documented weight-management pairing described by Barbara Bullard, while keeping adequate nourishment central. (reviewed); If a repeated eating pattern is the main concern, compare Appetite Choice with the distinct Habit Freedom practice. (reviewed); When deciding whether to have a treat, use the function as a moment for conscious choice rather than a rigid food rule. (reviewed)

Exploring a felt sense of calm and steadiness around the heart. (draft); Visualizing comfortable heart rhythm as a wellness exercise, not cardiovascular treatment. (draft); Explore Heart Flow and Body Tune-Up as separate practices; the 1990 wishlist specifically proposed that pairing for overnight listening. (reviewed); Compare Heart Flow with Circulation to distinguish their intended attention targets rather than treating them as medical interventions. (reviewed); At the end of a stressful day, use Heart Flow as a calm body-awareness reflection. (reviewed); During an easy, unforced breathing period, pair a calm heart-centered intention with ordinary breathing awareness. (reviewed)

Practicing calm awareness of the heart and blood vessels. (draft); Reflecting on relaxation and balance without using felt sensations as a blood-pressure measurement or treatment. (draft); Note how stressful situations feel in your body and compare the experience with a separate Relax session. (reviewed); Use a gentle bedtime relaxation intention while maintaining any prescribed monitoring and care. (reviewed)

Visualizing coordinated protective responses and a return to balance. (draft); Reflecting on immune readiness as an intention, not proof of protection from illness or a substitute for care. (draft); During a wellness meditation, imagine coordinated protective processes and a return to ordinary balance. (reviewed); Review the 1991 report describing Immunizing, Circulation and De-Discomfort as a historical combination, not a proven therapeutic protocol. (reviewed); Compare Immune Readiness with Body Tune-Up when choosing the intended theme for a nonmedical self-care session. (reviewed)

Exploring awareness of comfortable, unforced breathing. (draft); Visualizing respiratory maintenance without treating breathing difficulty or delaying medical help. (draft); While relaxed, notice easy, natural breathing without forcing a longer inhale, exhale or breath hold. (reviewed); After Relax, explore Breathe Better as a separate practice focused on respiratory comfort. (reviewed); Compare the focused breathing intention with the broader Body Tune-Up intention to choose which practice suits a quiet session. (reviewed)

Reflecting on the intention to make useful nourishment available from food. (draft); Exploring the distinction between sufficient nourishment and unnecessary retention as imagery, not a way to control metabolism or replace adequate eating. (draft); When choosing the Food More mode, reflect on adequate nourishment and a sense of receiving what you need from regular meals. (reviewed); When choosing the Food Less mode, reflect on satisfaction and avoiding unnecessary retention without restricting required nutrition. (reviewed); Explore Nutricia and Eat/No Eat together for a weight-management intention, as Barbara Bullard explicitly described in the 1993 Odyssey Part II account. (reviewed); In the existing OCF weight-management chain, use Nutricia before Appetite Choice, with Habit Freedom when needed and Detox as an optional separate final practice. (reviewed)

Practicing steadiness during personally experienced hormonal transitions. (draft); Reflecting on physical and emotional comfort without claiming to regulate hormone levels or replace care. (draft); For menopause-related changes, use this as an optional emotional and body-awareness reflection, separate from medical symptom management. (reviewed)

Reflecting on a personally desired level of sexual arousal. (draft); Practicing a shift of attention from unwanted arousal toward another chosen interest. (draft); Reflect on your own level of sexual interest and whether you want a subjective shift toward MORE or LESS. (reviewed)

Directing kind attention toward a chosen part of the body. (draft); Visualizing whole-body maintenance and renewal without claiming healing or replacing treatment. (draft); Use Body Tune-Up as a broad, nonmedical self-care exercise when no single body area is the intended focus. (reviewed); At the end of an active day, explore Body Tune-Up as a reflective practice before a separate Restorative Sleep session. (reviewed); When choosing between body-oriented functions, use Body Tune-Up for broad awareness rather than a specific Circulation or Seeing intention. (reviewed); Explore the 1990 requested Heart Flow and Tune-Up pairing as separate, optional practices for evening relaxation. (reviewed)

Imagining a chosen area of the body in a comfortable, renewed state. (draft); Exploring regeneration imagery without expecting tissue regrowth or substituting imagery for medical care. (draft); Compare Regenerate with Body Tune-Up to choose between a renewal theme and a maintenance theme. (reviewed); Explore Inner Power separately when the intended goal is confidence or vitality rather than physical regeneration imagery. (reviewed)

Comparing temporary, area-specific sensitivity imagery with general comfort practice. (draft); Reviewing the documented distinction between temporary numbing and its release, without suppressing warning signs or delaying care. (draft); For a nonurgent, minor itch, explore temporary changes in perceived sensation while staying aware of any underlying cause. (reviewed); If you practice temporary numbing, explicitly return to normal awareness afterward using the documented release procedure. (reviewed); Compare Temporary Numbing and Comfort so you can choose the appropriate nonmedical, reversible practice instead of treating them as interchangeable. (reviewed)

Reflecting on knowledge and experience already available to you. (draft); Inviting relevant information to mind while checking impressions against reliable sources when accuracy matters. (draft); When trying to remember a detail you have encountered before, use Information Access as a prompt to search your own memory and verify the result. (reviewed); During brainstorming, let relevant associations arise before checking them against your notes or other reliable sources. (reviewed); With a clearly stated question, explore what memories or intuitions feel relevant without assuming the answer is externally sourced knowledge. (reviewed); Compare Information Access with Recall: one invites broader associations, while the other targets remembered material. (reviewed); Record an apparent insight along with what you already knew and what would be needed to confirm it. (reviewed)

Preparing for mental arithmetic or number-based study. (draft); Practicing attention to numerical patterns while independently checking calculations. (draft); During routine mental arithmetic practice, work with simple numbers and check the answers afterward. (reviewed); While estimating a household budget, use the practice to keep attention on the numbers and verify totals with a calculator. (reviewed); Experiment with logical or symbolic reasoning exercises, an extension explicitly requested in the 1990 wishlist. (reviewed); Before a low-stakes math practice session, use the function as an intention for calmer engagement rather than as a substitute for learning the method. (reviewed); When making a quick numerical estimate, calculate mentally and then compare it with an exact result. (reviewed)

Making room for quiet reflection on a personal question. (draft); Exploring internal dialogue while distinguishing impressions from verified facts. (draft); Explore Contemplation as part of a grounding or centering practice, a use suggested in the 1990 wishlist. (reviewed); In a safe resting place outdoors, use Contemplation to observe concerns and settle before continuing an activity. (reviewed); Use a Contemplation session to examine a mental image or creative question without requiring unusual sensory experiences. (reviewed); Start with a clear question, use the documented opening command, and finish by using the appropriate closing command. (reviewed)

Giving deliberate attention to material you wish to remember. (draft); Comparing information capture with the separately documented recall application, without assuming memory is infallible. (draft); After studying a key concept, deliberately select it for Imprint and return to the material later to test retrieval. (reviewed); Use Imprint to remember when to use another learned function; a 1989 participant described doing this with Nutricia. (reviewed); After an important experience, select a few concrete details you want to remember and later compare your recollection with written notes. (reviewed); During foreign-language study, use Imprint with a small set of vocabulary and check retention during later recall practice. (reviewed); After deliberately imprinting selected information, use Recall at a later time to practice retrieving it. (reviewed)

Exploring alternatives when a decision feels narrow. (draft); Considering possible directions without treating imagined outcomes as predictions. (draft); When facing several plausible choices, use Options to list alternatives before deciding. (reviewed); While exploring a possible vocation change, use Options to brainstorm realistic alternatives and research them afterward. (reviewed); Before future-oriented visualization or planning, use Options to make room for more than one possible direction. (reviewed); When a project seems blocked, identify three alternative approaches before selecting a next step. (reviewed); Explore Options before Manifest when you want to compare possible goals before selecting one intention. (reviewed)

Inviting previously learned material to mind during study. (draft); Reflecting on a past experience while recognizing that recollection can be incomplete or mistaken. (draft); Before a practice quiz, use Recall to bring to mind material you have already learned, then verify your answer. (reviewed); While practicing a new language, try to retrieve previously learned words before looking at the answer. (reviewed); Try to remember a name or detail from a recent conversation and check your recollection if accuracy matters. (reviewed); Recall a constructive group experience or pleasant memory as part of a personal appreciation practice. (reviewed); After an Imprint session, return at a later interval and practice recall without treating a vivid memory as infallible. (reviewed)

Preparing for reasoning or problem-solving practice. (draft); Practicing organized attention to relevant details without equating speed with accuracy. (draft); Before a conversation, use Think Fast as a mental-fluency intention and take time to listen carefully as well. (reviewed); During a study session, compare Think Fast with Imprint to distinguish processing ideas from retaining them. (reviewed); During a short, low-stakes brainstorm, generate several options before evaluating their quality. (reviewed); While rehearsing foreign-language responses, explore Think Fast alongside ordinary speaking and retrieval practice. (reviewed)

Preparing to speak or read aloud with a sense of ease. (draft); Reflecting on clear expression before a conversation or presentation. (draft); Before answering a question in class or a meeting, use Speak Up as a confidence and expression intention. (reviewed); When you need to explain a concern respectfully, use Speak Up to prepare clear words rather than to control the other person's reaction. (reviewed); During foreign-language conversation practice, focus on expressing familiar material even if mistakes happen. (reviewed)

Reviewing the exercise's intention of calm during an injury response, alongside appropriate first aid. (draft); Reflecting on supportive awareness without postponing emergency services or professional care. (draft); After contacting emergency services or beginning appropriate first aid for an injury, use Injury Response only as an optional composure cue if it does not interrupt care. (reviewed); During a nonemergency rehearsal, review which real-world first-aid actions come before any optional self-regulation practice. (reviewed)

Reviewing the exercise as an intention of calm in a toxic-exposure context, not an antidote. (draft); Distinguishing a wellness intention from the need for prompt poison-control or emergency advice. (draft); For a possible toxic exposure, contact Poison Control or emergency services first; use Toxic Exposure Response only as an optional composure practice that does not delay assistance. (reviewed); While receiving professional exposure instructions, prioritize following them; any self-directed practice must remain secondary. (reviewed); During an emergency-readiness review, distinguish Toxic Exposure Response from the unrelated nonmedical Detox imagery function. (reviewed)

Reflecting on an emotion that is interfering with a chosen activity. (draft); Practicing a calmer relationship to a feeling without denying useful emotional information. (draft); After a frustrating interaction, explore Let Go to loosen initial anger before choosing what to do next. (reviewed); When a minor thought keeps pulling attention away from a task, use Let Go to shift attention without pretending the concern never existed. (reviewed); Before a consequential decision, make room for immediate emotions to settle and then revisit the actual evidence. (reviewed); Explore Let Go followed by Reset as separate practices; survey participants described using that pairing. (reviewed); During grief, use Let Go only for a selected moment of tension if wanted, without trying to erase meaningful feelings or memories. (reviewed)

Reflecting on a recurring thought that distracts from the present. (draft); Exploring release of an unwanted emotional pattern while retaining useful memories and personal choice. (draft); Identify a recurring thought that interferes with your goals and explore reducing its grip while retaining relevant learning. (reviewed); After a conflict continues to occupy attention, use Offload as a distinct longer-pattern practice rather than an immediate Let Go substitute. (reviewed); During a period of loss, explore Offload for specific overwhelming mental patterns while preserving memory and allowing feelings to be present. (reviewed); When working on a chosen habit, explore Offload for recurring thoughts that make the behavior harder to change. (reviewed)

Reflecting on another being's possible perspective with openness. (draft); Preparing for attentive communication without assuming access to private thoughts or certainty about another's experience. (draft); Before a conversation, reflect on what another person might be experiencing without assuming you know their thoughts. (reviewed); During disagreement, use Empathize as a reminder to listen and ask questions before offering conclusions. (reviewed); Explore Empathize when trying to respond thoughtfully to someone who is disappointed or stressed. (reviewed); After a perspective-taking reflection, use Speak Up to communicate your own needs clearly and respectfully. (reviewed); When spending time with an animal, observe its actual behavior and practice respectful attention rather than assuming telepathic understanding. (reviewed)

Clarifying a personally chosen outcome and desired completion time. (draft); Exploring a felt or imagined fulfilled intention without treating it as a guarantee of external events. (draft); Choose a concrete goal and a realistic completion time, then identify the actions needed to work toward it. (reviewed); For a pile of paperwork or assignments, set an intention to finish a defined portion by a selected time, as Barbara Bullard described for grading. (reviewed); After considering several alternatives with Options, use Manifest for the one future condition you actually choose. (reviewed); While reviewing personal finances, set an intention for a responsible planning action rather than expecting a financial outcome without action. (reviewed)

Exploring an imagined whole-body zone of temperature comfort. (draft); Reviewing adjustable comfort imagery without substituting it for suitable clothing, shelter, or protection from heat and cold. (draft); On an ordinary outdoor break, use temperature-comfort imagery only as a supplement to appropriate clothing and weather precautions. (reviewed); Before resting in an unfamiliar room, explore a comfortable temperature intention while also adjusting the actual bedding or thermostat. (reviewed)

Reflecting on a selected unwanted belief or expectation. (draft); Exploring release of a recurring pattern while preserving useful learning. (draft); Identify one specific limiting belief and reflect on a more realistic alternative that preserves what you have learned. (reviewed); After noticing a repeating reaction to uncertainty, explore loosening the reaction without claiming it will eliminate risk. (reviewed); Use Dissolve for a clearly chosen belief or response, and select Offload instead when the target is recurring mental interference. (reviewed)

Imagining calm personal space during unwanted insect contact. (draft); Reflecting on the distinction between discouraging contact and intentionally observing, without replacing practical insect protection. (draft)

Considering a question with openness to quiet impressions. (draft); Reflecting on possible guidance while checking facts and retaining responsibility for decisions. (draft); When you notice a strong hunch, record it and later check whether it corresponded to verifiable information. (reviewed); Compare a waking intuitive impression with a separate Sleep Insight question, recording what actually happened afterward. (reviewed)

Practising with a chosen intention and deciding whether to keep the ball around you or draw it back within. (draft); Practising with the familiar personal ball before trying an optional larger extent. (draft)

Recalling a personal sense of vitality and available resources. (draft); Exploring how to direct a felt sense of energy toward a chosen purpose. (draft); Before a routine task that calls for enthusiasm, use Access to Energy as an intention for readiness. (reviewed)

Choosing one activity to receive sustained attention. (draft); Preparing for focused study or deliberate engagement with an experience. (draft); Before reading a course chapter, use Focus to direct attention to the selected material. (reviewed); After an interruption while coding, choose the next concrete problem and use Focus to return attention to it. (reviewed); During safe skills practice such as walking a familiar path, keep attention on the immediate task and surroundings. (reviewed); While reading something challenging, use Focus to keep attention on the current passage, taking breaks as needed. (reviewed); Before using Imprint during study, use Focus as a separate attention-setting practice. (reviewed)

Choosing a brief rest when it is safe and appropriate to sleep. (draft); Reflecting on the intention to wake from a short rest feeling refreshed, without replacing adequate sleep. (draft); After a short rest, use Quick Recharge to return to a routine activity feeling more ready to engage. (reviewed); During a sluggish morning, compare Quick Recharge with Reset before choosing which intention fits the moment. (reviewed)

Taking time to explore physical ease and reduced unnecessary tension. (draft); Practicing a quiet transition from mental busyness toward rest. (draft); Before a presentation or language-practice session, use Relax to settle ordinary nervousness. (reviewed); During an evening wind-down, use Relax to shift out of the day's activity before sleep. (reviewed); Following a frustrating conversation, use Relax to notice and release physical tension before deciding what to say next. (reviewed); Before focused study, use Relax as an optional preparatory stage rather than duplicating a full induction inside a chain. (reviewed); During a safe rest stop, use Relax and Contemplation separately to settle anticipatory worry, as a historical hiker described. (reviewed)

Reflecting on a desired shift from weariness toward renewed engagement. (draft); Practicing an intention of clarity and confidence without ignoring persistent fatigue or emotional distress. (draft); When feeling temporarily flat or worn down, use Reset to orient toward a clearer, more active state. (reviewed); After waking from ordinary sleep, use Reset as a deliberate transition into daytime activity. (reviewed); After using Let Go for immediate frustration, explore Reset as a separate reorientation practice. (reviewed); Before the first planned activity of the day, use Reset as an intention to become more alert and ready. (reviewed); Choose Reset when the goal is to shift out of an unwanted state, and Quick Recharge when the goal is a brief refresh. (reviewed)

Reviewing how a current temporary application differs from the learned ability. (draft); Reflecting on placing a selected application on hold when its purpose is complete, using only its documented scope. (draft); When a temporary function application is complete, use the appropriate documented release or closing action rather than leaving it ambiguous. (reviewed); If a practice feels overstimulating, stop and return to ordinary surroundings; historical users described Release as part of ending activation. (reviewed); Check whether a particular function has its own Cancel or close command; do not assume a general Release is interchangeable. (reviewed)

Recognizing a specific unwanted repeated behavior. (draft); Reflecting on a chosen change in a habit without treating the exercise as a substitute for needed professional support. (draft); When addressing an unwanted automatic snack routine, identify the specific behavior and choose an alternative response that respects genuine hunger. (reviewed); If you routinely delay starting a chosen task, use Habit Freedom as a reflection on the recurring pattern and practice a small replacement step. (reviewed); For a chosen smoking-cessation goal, use Habit Freedom only as optional motivation alongside evidence-based cessation support. (reviewed); When reflecting on recurring impulsive financial decisions, use Habit Freedom to recognize the pattern and create a concrete independent decision rule. (reviewed)

Preparing to begin a chosen task with a clear next action. (draft); Renewing an intention to continue or complete an activity. (draft); After choosing one manageable next step, use Do This Now to begin rather than continuing to plan. (reviewed); When you notice yourself repeatedly postponing a low-stakes task, pick a two-minute starting action and begin it. (reviewed); After exploring alternatives, select one practical action and use Do This Now as a transition into execution. (reviewed); Before a study block, put the materials in front of you and begin the first exercise instead of rehearsing the whole workload. (reviewed); At the beginning of a work period, choose a single priority and act on its first step. (reviewed)

Reflecting on personal resources when facing a challenge. (draft); Practicing a calm sense of inner strength in daily life without assuming extraordinary abilities. (draft); Before a presentation, reflect on personal strengths and then prepare to communicate clearly. (reviewed); After a disappointing result, use Inner Power to reconnect with your existing resources and choose a constructive next action. (reviewed); Before a social interaction, use Inner Power as a subjective confidence practice without expecting to control others. (reviewed); Before a practice examination, explore confidence and Recall as distinct goals, keeping answer accuracy separate from self-belief. (reviewed); Before an important day, name a capability you already have and use Inner Power to focus on exercising it. (reviewed)

Exploring a felt sense of smooth, coordinated movement. (draft); Preparing attentive movement practice while respecting physical limits and safe conditions. (draft); During safe movement practice, explore a sense of smooth rhythm while remaining attentive to the environment. (reviewed); Before a familiar sport drill, use Coordination as an intention for steadier, more fluid movement. (reviewed); Compare Coordination with Light Foot when deciding whether the goal is rhythm or ease of movement. (reviewed)

Bringing attention to lighter, quieter steps in ordinary movement. (draft); Reflecting on ease and precision in walking without assuming protection from falls or injury. (draft); During comfortable walking practice, use Light Foot as an intention for ease and smoothness, not as physical protection. (reviewed); Before a familiar sport's footwork drill, rehearse a feeling of light, controlled movement. (reviewed); Compare Light Foot with Coordination to choose between lightness and rhythm as your immediate focus. (reviewed); At a rest stop during a hike, reflect on relaxed foot placement while prioritizing terrain awareness and ordinary safety. (reviewed)

Reflecting on the tone and experiences you would like for the coming day. (draft); Clarifying daily intentions without expecting control over other people or external events. (draft); At the beginning of the day, choose a practical tone or intention for how you want to respond to events. (reviewed); Choose kindness or appreciation as a theme for how you want to engage with other people today. (reviewed); When beginning a busy workday, choose a workable priority rather than treating the function as a substitute for planning. (reviewed)

Reviewing the exercise's intention of prompt, coordinated action. (draft); Reflecting on the temporary response ending when the immediate need passes, without assuming exceptional strength or taking physical risks. (draft); During appropriately supervised sport practice, use Strong-Quick as a confidence intention for a familiar strength-and-speed drill. (reviewed); Before a routine, correctly loaded lifting task, focus on sound technique rather than attempting extraordinary strength. (reviewed)

Exploring attention to sounds or remembered sound. (draft); Comparing inward listening with imaginative sound experience without claiming hearing restoration or ignoring environmental warnings. (draft); During a quiet conversation or lecture, use Hearing MORE as an intention for attentive listening, not as a change in actual hearing acuity. (reviewed); When identifying an everyday sound in a safe setting, deliberately attend to its characteristics and then check the source. (reviewed); In a distracting environment, explore Hearing LESS only as a subjective attention practice while retaining awareness of important sounds. (reviewed); Compare Hearing LESS with Sleep Easy for noisy sleep surroundings while still using practical noise-control measures. (reviewed); While listening at a safe volume, focus on one instrument or pattern and notice details you had not attended to before. (reviewed)

Exploring remembered or deliberately imagined visual detail in your own way. (draft); Practicing attention to seeing without treating imagery as vision correction or requiring vivid mental pictures. (draft); During a safe visual-observation exercise, notice shapes, contrast and details without assuming a change in eyesight. (reviewed); During creative planning, imagine an object and deliberately change one feature of the image. (reviewed); After viewing a diagram, picture its main parts and compare your visualization with the original. (reviewed); Before drawing or making artwork, mentally rehearse colors, layout and composition. (reviewed); Explore Seeing and Hearing as separate complementary perception practices; the 1990 wishlist proposed pairing them on a recording. (reviewed)

Exploring memories of familiar aromas. (draft); Reflecting on attention to scent without using the exercise to judge whether air or a substance is safe. (draft); While smelling a familiar, safe aroma, use Smell MORE to notice subtle differences in the experience. (reviewed); In an ordinary setting with an unpleasant but nonhazardous smell, explore Smell LESS as an attention-shifting intention. (reviewed); Compare Smell and Taste as separate sensory-awareness exercises without promising improved sensory function. (reviewed)

Exploring familiar flavor memories during sensory reflection. (draft); Bringing deliberate attention to taste without using it as a food-safety test. (draft); When sampling a safe food, use Taste MORE to attend to flavor and texture details. (reviewed); While evaluating a familiar recipe, compare small differences in flavor without judging food safety by taste. (reviewed); When a safe food tastes unusually intense, explore Taste LESS as a subjective attention practice. (reviewed); Explore Taste and Smell in separate sessions to notice how flavor attention and aroma attention differ. (reviewed)

Exploring remembered textures or an imagined sense of touch. (draft); Practicing attention to skin sensations without suppressing warning signs or assuming protection from harm. (draft); While handling a safe object, use Touch MORE to attend to its texture, temperature and pressure. (reviewed); During a craft or art activity, use Touch MORE to notice the feel of tools and materials. (reviewed); In a safe environment with nonhazardous tactile distraction, use Touch LESS as a brief subjective attention shift while preserving awareness of injury risks. (reviewed)

Setting an intention of restorative rest before sleep. (draft); Reflecting on a sense of renewal without assuming sleep imagery treats illness or replaces care. (draft); Before an ordinary night's sleep, use Restorative Sleep as a rest-and-recovery intention. (reviewed); After a demanding day, explore Body Tune-Up and then Restorative Sleep as separate self-care exercises. (reviewed); At bedtime, set aside the day's tasks and focus on the experience of restorative rest without requiring a particular sleep outcome. (reviewed); For familiar minor discomfort at night, compare Comfort with Restorative Sleep as separate practices, without ignoring symptoms. (reviewed)

Preparing for natural sleep in a safe place. (draft); Reflecting on a desired waking time without relying on the exercise instead of an alarm when timing matters. (draft); When ready for bed, use Sleep as a deliberate transition away from waking activity. (reviewed); After a separate evening Relax practice, use Sleep to focus on natural sleep onset. (reviewed); If you plan a dream-themed evening routine, use Dream Theme to choose the theme before a separate Sleep practice. (reviewed)

Choosing a personally meaningful dream theme. (draft); Reflecting on dream recall after waking without assuming dreams report external facts. (draft); Before bedtime, choose a comfortable subject you would like to explore in a dream. (reviewed); Use Dream Theme to suggest a gentle setting or story idea for imaginative dreaming. (reviewed); On waking, record anything you remember about your dreams without assuming that their content was controlled. (reviewed); Compare Dream Theme with Sleep Insight: one concerns dream content, while the other concerns reflecting on a question. (reviewed)

Considering a question you would like to reflect on through sleep. (draft); Reviewing morning impressions as possible ideas rather than verified answers or instructions. (draft); Before sleep, select one manageable question and note whether any useful idea emerges on waking. (reviewed); When stuck on a creative or technical problem, record the question before bed and check any morning ideas against reality. (reviewed); Keep a notebook nearby to record a possible insight, including nights when no answer appears. (reviewed); Compare Sleep Insight with Contemplation when you want additional reflection on a choice. (reviewed)

Preparing for rest in unfamiliar but safe surroundings. (draft); Reflecting on returning to sleep after ordinary distractions while remaining responsive to genuine safety needs. (draft); In a safe unfamiliar sleeping environment, use Sleep Easy to support settling into ordinary sleep. (reviewed); When harmless background noise makes settling difficult, use Sleep Easy alongside practical noise management. (reviewed); After waking unexpectedly, use Sleep Easy to return attention to natural sleep without forcing it. (reviewed); During travel, use Sleep Easy as part of a familiar bedtime ritual while respecting actual rest needs. (reviewed); Explore Hearing LESS separately for distracting sounds if appropriate, while preserving awareness of alarms and hazards. (reviewed)

Reviewing the intention of short-term alertness when an immediate need arises. (draft); Distinguishing a felt alertness practice from adequate sleep; never relying on it to make drowsy driving or hazardous work safe. (draft); Before an ordinary activity requiring attentiveness, use Stay Awake as an intention for alert engagement when you are already adequately rested. (reviewed); Review historical alertness stories critically: if you are sleepy while driving or operating machinery, stop and rest rather than using Stay Awake to push through. (reviewed)
